routes.title: From a polynomial to its Galois group
routes.audience: A first course in field theory
routes.goal: Prove irreducibility, obtain permutation information, and finish a complete group determination.
routes.checkpoint: Give a proof of \(\operatorname{Gal}(x^5-x-1/\mathbb Q)=S_5\) and state exactly what each prime contributes.

steps.title: Fields, factors, and the action on roots
steps.note: Fix the ground field, separate irreducibility from separability, and translate factorization into a permutation action.

steps.title: Irreducibility by reduction modulo primes
steps.note: Use one finite-field factorization, or intersect the possible degrees supplied by several primes. Understand why the method can fail for an irreducible polynomial.

steps.title: Frobenius: from factor degrees to permutations
steps.note: A factorization over a finite field reveals a cycle type in a global Galois group. Combine these local witnesses with a separate group-theoretic argument.

steps.title: The group-theoretic step: transitivity, alternating groups, and symmetric groups
steps.note: Local arithmetic supplies permutations. Block systems, transpositions, and long cycles explain when those permutations force a large group.

steps.title: Discriminants, parity, and ramification
steps.note: The discriminant detects collisions of roots and the sign character of a Galois group. Its square class is powerful, but it does not measure the size of the group.

steps.title: Checkpoint
steps.note: Give a proof of \(\operatorname{Gal}(x^5-x-1/\mathbb Q)=S_5\) and state exactly what each prime contributes.

routes.title: From valuations to large groups
routes.audience: Readers comfortable with valuations and finite permutation groups
routes.goal: Learn how coefficient divisibility restricts factor degrees and produces long prime cycles.
routes.checkpoint: Separate the irreducibility input, the Newton-polygon input, Jordan's theorem, and the discriminant step.

steps.title: Schönemann–Eisenstein and one-edge Newton polygons
steps.note: A divisibility pattern can force every factor to have the full degree. Translation and Newton slopes extend the elementary criterion.

steps.title: Newton polygons, factor degrees, and large cycles
steps.note: Read p-adic root valuations from coefficients, intersect the permitted factor degrees, and use suitable slope denominators to force a large Galois group.

steps.title: The group-theoretic step: transitivity, alternating groups, and symmetric groups
steps.note: Local arithmetic supplies permutations. Block systems, transpositions, and long cycles explain when those permutations force a large group.

steps.title: Taylor truncations: two exact benchmarks
steps.note: Exponential truncations have alternating or symmetric groups, while geometric truncations are cyclotomic. Their contrast identifies which arithmetic features a general truncation theory must track.

steps.title: Generalized Laguerre polynomials: two parameter regimes
steps.note: Factorial products connect local slopes to large Galois groups. Fixing the parameter and increasing the degree is a different problem from fixing the degree and varying the parameter.

steps.title: Checkpoint
steps.note: Separate the irreducibility input, the Newton-polygon input, Jordan's theorem, and the discriminant step.

routes.title: Study a structured family
routes.audience: Researchers moving from examples to a family theorem
routes.goal: Identify forced factors and symmetries before choosing the expected Galois group.
routes.checkpoint: Write the normalization, the natural ambient permutation group, a proved benchmark, and a source-scoped unresolved question.

steps.title: Reciprocal symmetry and the group on root pairs
steps.note: Pass from a reciprocal polynomial to a polynomial of half the degree. The remaining quadratic extensions explain both irreducibility and the correct ambient Galois group.

steps.title: Sparse polynomials, factor reversal, and large gaps
steps.note: Separate persistent reciprocal factors from the nonreciprocal part, then use coefficient sparsity to constrain possible factorizations.

steps.title: Trinomials: uniform families and explicit classifications
steps.note: The polynomials xⁿ−x−1 realize Sₙ in every degree. Prime reductions give short certificates, while inertia explains the uniform theorem.

steps.title: Eulerian polynomials: descents, shifts, and inverse pairs
steps.note: Descent statistics lead to reciprocal polynomials. A prime-index Eisenstein argument and an exact quartic example show how combinatorics, local arithmetic, and Galois theory fit together.

steps.title: Fekete polynomials: character sums and reciprocal arithmetic
steps.note: Quadratic characters impose exact rational factors and reciprocal symmetry. Trace polynomials connect their irreducibility and Galois groups to special values and square classes.

steps.title: Hermite, Bessel, and Legendre: shared tools, different answers
steps.note: Classical polynomial families share differential and recurrence identities, but their arithmetic factorization problems differ. Parity reduction and coefficient products expose the correct questions.

steps.title: Checkpoint
steps.note: Write the normalization, the natural ambient permutation group, a proved benchmark, and a source-scoped unresolved question.

routes.title: Read probabilistic results without changing the model
routes.audience: Researchers reading counting and random-polynomial papers
routes.goal: Keep the asymptotic parameter, coefficient law, conditioning, and analytic hypotheses visible.
routes.checkpoint: Explain why a fixed-degree height theorem does not imply a growing-degree fair-sign theorem.

steps.title: Counting exceptional Galois groups by height
steps.note: At fixed degree, almost all integer polynomials have full symmetric group. The sharp exceptional order, and its change under reciprocity, reveal which arithmetic obstructions dominate.

steps.title: Random polynomials: models and proof strategies
steps.note: The coefficient law and the limiting parameter determine the problem. A guide to irreducibility, alternating-group containment, and the additional step needed for a full symmetric group.

steps.title: Littlewood polynomials: signs, parity, and special degrees
steps.note: Independent signs create strong congruence constraints. Exact examples show both their usefulness and why the all-degree probabilistic problem needs more than reduction modulo two.

steps.title: Random reciprocal polynomials of growing degree
steps.note: Independent free coefficients generate paired roots and a signed-permutation group. The trace polynomial connects this structured model to ordinary factorization problems.

steps.title: Characteristic polynomials of random matrices
steps.note: Matrix entries can be independent while characteristic-polynomial coefficients are strongly dependent. Local rank estimates replace the independent-coefficient tools.

steps.title: Checkpoint
steps.note: Explain why a fixed-degree height theorem does not imply a growing-degree fair-sign theorem.

routes.title: From generic families to arithmetic specializations
routes.audience: Graduate readers interested in arithmetic geometry and inverse Galois theory
routes.goal: Connect generic monodromy, Hilbert irreducibility, and specialization while tracking the quantifiers.
routes.checkpoint: Distinguish infinitely many good specializations, all but finitely many, density one, and an infinite tower.

steps.title: Critical points and monodromy: a geometric route to the symmetric group
steps.note: Derivatives and critical values determine the generic group; the cubic example separates that group from four different rational fibers.

steps.title: Specialization and Hilbert irreducibility
steps.note: Pass from a polynomial over a rational function field to arithmetic fibers, and understand how the exceptional parameters are organized.

steps.title: Inverse Galois theory and generic polynomials
steps.note: Construct a polynomial with a prescribed group, then distinguish one realization from regular families and universal parametrizations.

steps.title: Composition, iteration, and arboreal groups
steps.note: Use extension towers and rooted trees to study repeated polynomial composition. Separate stability from maximality of the Galois action.

steps.title: Generalized Laguerre polynomials: two parameter regimes
steps.note: Factorial products connect local slopes to large Galois groups. Fixing the parameter and increasing the degree is a different problem from fixing the degree and varying the parameter.

steps.title: Checkpoint
steps.note: Distinguish infinitely many good specializations, all but finitely many, density one, and an infinite tower.

routes.title: Turn a computation into a certificate
routes.audience: Readers using computer algebra in proofs
routes.goal: Understand the algebra behind factorization and group algorithms and record what has been proved.
routes.checkpoint: Record the exact input, software version, field, factorization or resolvent witness, and certification step.

steps.title: Irreducibility over finite fields
steps.note: Turn Frobenius powers into exact irreducibility certificates, count irreducibles, and distinguish irreducible from primitive polynomials.

steps.title: Exact factorization: finite fields, Hensel lifting, and lattices
steps.note: Factorization algorithms turn structural ideas into certificates: Frobenius and linear algebra over finite fields, then p-adic lifting and lattice reduction over the rationals.

steps.title: Resolvents: turn group containment into factorization
steps.note: A resolvent records how a group acts on selected expressions in the roots. Rational factors can detect a hidden partition or force descent to a smaller subgroup.

steps.title: Computing a Galois group with a proof certificate
steps.note: A reliable computation combines exact arithmetic, subgroup constraints, and certification. Save enough evidence that the conclusion survives a change of software.

steps.title: Checkpoint
steps.note: Record the exact input, software version, field, factorization or resolvent witness, and certification step.

methods.question: Is a given polynomial irreducible over Q?
methods.signal: A useful factorization modulo a small prime
methods.method: Degree-preserving reduction and intersection of possible factor degrees
methods.output: An exact irreducibility certificate when the remaining proper degrees are eliminated
methods.boundary: An irreducible polynomial need not have an irreducible reduction at any prime.
methods.input: A useful factorization modulo a small prime

methods.question: Can coefficient divisibility prove irreducibility?
methods.signal: One prime divides all lower coefficients, or the valuations have a simple pattern
methods.output: Irreducibility over a local field, hence over Q, or restrictions on factor degrees
methods.boundary: A criterion is sufficient; failure of its hypotheses is not evidence of reducibility.
methods.input: One prime divides all lower coefficients, or the valuations have a simple pattern

methods.question: Can several local tests work together?
methods.signal: Different primes exclude different factor degrees
methods.output: A global irreducibility proof even when each individual prime permits factors
methods.boundary: The same polygons may still leave common possible degrees.
methods.input: Different primes exclude different factor degrees

methods.question: Can root sizes rule out factors?
methods.signal: A monic integer polynomial satisfying Perron's coefficient inequality, or a root bound at a prime-valued argument
methods.method: Perron's criterion and archimedean factor bounds
methods.output: Irreducibility from root location and integral constant terms or factor evaluations
methods.boundary: Perron's test needs monicity and a nonzero constant term; the displayed bounds are strict.
methods.input: A monic integer polynomial satisfying Perron's coefficient inequality, or a root bound at a prime-valued argument

methods.question: Can integer evaluations rule out every factor?
methods.signal: Many distinct integer arguments with small nonzero values, or at least 2n+1 unit or prime values for a primitive degree-n polynomial
methods.method: Schur unit-value arguments, Pólya interpolation, and prime-value counting
methods.output: An exact irreducibility certificate from restrictions on the values of hypothetical integral factors
methods.boundary: Use the stated degree-dependent threshold and distinct arguments; one prime value alone is insufficient.
methods.input: Many distinct integer arguments with small nonzero values, or at least 2n+1 unit or prime values for a primitive degree-n polynomial

methods.question: Is a composition or binomial irreducible?
methods.signal: An irreducible outer polynomial F, a nonconstant inner polynomial g, or a binomial in characteristic zero
methods.method: Capelli root-field reduction and the exact binomial power criterion
methods.output: A lower-degree irreducibility question over a root field; for binomials, necessary and sufficient power exclusions
methods.boundary: Irreducibility of both inputs is insufficient. Binomials with exponent divisible by 4 require the exceptional negative-four-times-a-fourth-power exclusion.
methods.input: An irreducible outer polynomial F, a nonconstant inner polynomial g, or a binomial in characteristic zero

methods.question: What happens when a sparse polynomial has a large gap?
methods.signal: A family x^N c(x^{-1})+d(x) with fixed end pieces
methods.output: Irreducibility of a specified nonreciprocal part for sufficiently large N
methods.boundary: Reciprocal factors and Capellian exceptions cannot be discarded silently.
methods.input: A family x^N c(x^{-1})+d(x) with fixed end pieces

methods.question: Which permutations occur in the Galois group?
methods.signal: Squarefree factorization at a prime of good reduction
methods.output: An element of the specified cycle type
methods.boundary: Bad primes and unseen cycle types require separate treatment.
methods.input: Squarefree factorization at a prime of good reduction

methods.question: When does cycle evidence force A_n or S_n?
methods.signal: Transitivity, primitivity, and an appropriate prime cycle or transposition
methods.output: A proved group containment or equality
methods.boundary: A transitive subgroup containing a transposition need not be \(S_n\).
methods.input: Transitivity, primitivity, and an appropriate prime cycle or transposition

methods.question: How can A_n be distinguished from S_n?
methods.signal: Containment of \(A_n\) has already been proved
methods.method: Discriminant square class or an odd permutation
methods.boundary: A nonsquare discriminant alone does not prove \(S_n\).
methods.input: Containment of \(A_n\) has already been proved

methods.question: Does a root symmetry force a smaller ambient group?
methods.output: A wreath-product or other structural upper bound
methods.boundary: A generic \(S_n\) expectation can be incompatible with the root symmetry.

methods.question: How can remaining candidate groups be separated?
methods.signal: Several subgroups fit the observed Frobenius types
methods.method: Resolvents, relative invariants, and subgroup descent
methods.output: Additional exact constraints or a certified group
methods.boundary: Numerical approximation and a plausible candidate are not by themselves a proof.
methods.input: Several subgroups fit the observed Frobenius types

methods.question: Do generic results survive parameter specialization?
methods.signal: An irreducible family over Q(t), or over K(t) with K Hilbertian
methods.method: Hilbert irreducibility and specialized geometric criteria
methods.output: Many good specializations under the stated hypotheses
methods.boundary: Infinitely many, density one, and all but finitely many are different conclusions.
methods.input: An irreducible family over Q(t), or over K(t) with K Hilbertian

methods.question: Are all iterates irreducible?
methods.signal: A polynomial f and the tower of its iterates
methods.method: Capelli-type steps, critical orbits, and arboreal groups
methods.output: Finite-level or all-level conclusions only under the relevant hypotheses
methods.boundary: Specializing each finite level does not select one specialization valid at every level.
methods.input: A polynomial f and the tower of its iterates

methods.question: Can an irreducible polynomial over F_q be constructed or certified?
methods.signal: Specified degree and possibly prescribed coefficients
methods.method: Frobenius congruences, gcd tests, and finite-field constructions
methods.output: A finite-field irreducibility certificate or an existence theorem
methods.boundary: Primitive is stronger than irreducible; an irreducible degree-n polynomial has cyclic splitting-field group.
methods.input: Specified degree and possibly prescribed coefficients

methods.question: Is a multivariate polynomial absolutely irreducible?
methods.signal: Sparse exponent support or an effective specialization problem
methods.output: Irreducibility after extending the coefficient field to an algebraic closure
methods.boundary: Exclude monomial factors; this differs from ordinary irreducibility over the ground field.
methods.input: Sparse exponent support or an effective specialization problem

methods.question: What does a random-polynomial theorem actually apply to?
methods.signal: A coefficient law and a specified limiting parameter
methods.method: Local mixing, sieve methods, and factor exclusion
methods.output: A probability estimate for the exact model in the theorem
methods.boundary: Track conditioning, \(A_n\) versus \(S_n\), and any RH or GRH hypothesis.
methods.input: A coefficient law and a specified limiting parameter

methods.question: What is the generic Galois group of F(X)−T?
methods.signal: Simple critical points with pairwise distinct critical values in characteristic zero
methods.input: Simple critical points with pairwise distinct critical values in characteristic zero
methods.method: Morse criterion: finite branch inertia generates transpositions
methods.output: Geometric and arithmetic group \(S_n\); a regular splitting field
methods.boundary: A full generic group does not determine every rational fiber. Check specialization separately.
